_comment: One entry per stage of the walk, in walk order. The walk (home page), the chapter pages, the chapters index and the atlas are all views of this list. `id` is the stage's anchor on the home page; `chapter` names its chapter page when it has one. `buildsOn` orders reading but never locks anything. `recall` holds explain-it-back prompts whose answers are in the lesson itself.

strands.label: structure
strands.blurb: How the atoms are joined: the network, its breaks and what fills them.

strands.label: flow
strands.blurb: Viscosity and the glass transition: how a melt stiffens and what that leaves behind.

strands.label: stress
strands.blurb: Strain frozen in by cooling, and how polarized light shows it.

strands.label: absorption
strands.blurb: Light taken out by ions, particles and band gaps, compounding with path length.

strands.label: emission
strands.blurb: Light given back: thermal glow and fluorescence.

strands.label: light at surfaces
strands.blurb: Refraction, dispersion and interference: color with nothing absorbed.

strands.label: seeing
strands.blurb: A color is a spectrum through a lamp and an eye.

strands.label: over time
strands.blurb: What water and years do to a glass.

lessons.name: the material
lessons.title: Glass is a liquid that stopped
lessons.claim: A silicate melt stiffens smoothly instead of crystallizing. The network keeps the liquid's disorder, and one viscosity curve runs the studio.

recall.q: Why does adding soda make a silica melt flow at a lower temperature?
recall.a: Each Na₂O brings an extra oxygen that cuts a bridge between two tetrahedra into two non-bridging oxygens. With fewer bridges the network is looser, so it flows at lower temperature.

recall.q: Lime and soda both break bridges. Why does lime make the glass last instead of dissolve?
recall.a: A Ca²⁺ ion holds two non-bridging oxygens at once and moves far less readily than Na⁺, so the glass stops leaching in water. Soda–silica glass alone dissolves; it is sold as water glass.

recall.q: Two pieces of the same batch were cooled at different rates. Which has the higher glass transition temperature, and why?
recall.a: The one cooled faster. Tg is where the melt's relaxation time outgrows the time cooling allows, so faster cooling makes the structure freeze in sooner, at a higher temperature, looser and less dense.

recall.q: Name the viscosity points from runniest to stiffest and what each is for.
recall.a: Melting (bubbles rise out), working (holds a shape on the pipe), softening (a hanging fiber stretches under its own weight), annealing (stress relaxes in minutes), strain (stress takes hours; below it nothing moves on a human timescale).

recall.q: Do medieval windows flow? What is the evidence?
recall.a: No. Extrapolated viscosity gives room-temperature relaxation times near 10³² years (Zanotto 1998), and Westminster Abbey glass would flow about a nanometer in a billion years (Gulbiten et al. 2018). The thick bottoms come from hand-flattened cylinder glass set heavy edge down.

lessons.name: the batch
lessons.title: Clear glass is not clear
lessons.claim: A trace of iron turns a pane's edge green, because absorption compounds with path length. The oxide bench shows how the recipe sets every property.

lessons.name: the melt
lessons.title: The furnace air picks the color
lessons.claim: Oxidizing or reducing air sets how much iron sits as Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺, and the two ions absorb differently.

lessons.name: the melt, long and short
lessons.title: Some glasses are long, some short
lessons.claim: Fragility measures how steeply viscosity rises near Tg, and it sets how long a glass stays workable.

lessons.name: the color rod
lessons.title: Each ion absorbs its own bands
lessons.claim: Each transition-metal or rare-earth ion takes its own bands out of the spectrum, and a blown piece is colored by its own wall thickness.

recall.q: What in a cobalt ion absorbs the light, and what sets which colors it takes?
recall.a: Its outer d-electrons, lifted between energy levels by light of particular energies. The surrounding glass sets the spacing of those levels, so the same ion absorbs differently in different hosts.

recall.q: Chromium absorbs at both ends of the spectrum. Why is chrome glass green?
recall.a: Cr⁶⁺ takes the violet edge and Cr³⁺ takes blue and orange-red, so what passes is the window between them, in the green.

recall.q: A solid-color bowl is palest at the rim and darkest at the foot. Why, and how does casing fix it?
recall.a: Each point is colored by the glass a ray crosses there (Beer–Lambert), and the rim is blown thinnest while the foot is heaviest. Casing puts the color in a thin skin of strong glass, so every part crosses about the same amount of color however the clear inside was blown.

recall.q: Why does solid cane look darkest down its middle while cased cane looks darkest at its edges?
recall.a: A ray through the middle of solid cane crosses the most glass. In cased cane the color is only in the skin: a ray down the middle crosses the skin twice, but a ray near the edge runs along the skin for a long way.

recall.q: Neodymium glass is lilac in daylight. Predict what happens under a tri-phosphor tube, and why.
recall.a: It turns blue-gray. Its absorption bands are narrow, and a tri-phosphor tube puts its light in a few narrow lines that the bands hit unevenly, so a different share of the lamp survives. The showroom stage shows it.

lessons.name: the glory hole
lessons.title: At heat, glass gives back what it takes
lessons.claim: Hot glass glows with emissivity equal to its absorptance (Kirchhoff), so a colorant that absorbs a band also glows in it.

lessons.name: the reheat
lessons.title: Some colors must be struck
lessons.claim: Gold ruby and cadmium reds appear only after a reheat grows particles or crystals: plasmon absorption and band-gap edges.

lessons.name: the lehr
lessons.title: Glass remembers how it cooled
lessons.claim: Uneven cooling freezes in stress, which makes glass birefringent; crossed polarizers turn that into interference colors.

lessons.name: the cold shop
lessons.title: Color with no colorant
lessons.claim: Dichroic coatings reflect one band by thin-film interference and pass its complement; nothing is absorbed.

lessons.name: the cold shop, cut
lessons.title: Clear glass holds every color
lessons.claim: Refractive index climbs toward the ultraviolet, so a cut glass splits white light; lead raises the dispersion, and crown and flint can cancel it.

lessons.name: the rack
lessons.title: Every color on the shelf
lessons.claim: Working backwards from a swatch to a melt has many answers, because three numbers cannot fix a spectrum.

lessons.name: the showroom
lessons.title: One glass gives light back
lessons.claim: Uranium glass fluoresces green under ultraviolet, and neodymium glass changes color from lamp to lamp.

lessons.name: the showroom, other eyes
lessons.title: Color is a fact about an eye
lessons.claim: Every color on the site is a spectrum through a lamp and an observer; change the observer and matches break.
